html:
A rising of peasants in Bengal in 1859 and 1860 against European planters who forced them to grow indigo, the blue dye plant.

Under the system, planters advanced small loans and made farmers sow indigo on their best land, then paid far below the market price. Debts passed from year to year. Those who refused were beaten, locked up or had their crops destroyed by the planters' men. In 1859 farmers in Nadia and nearby districts simply stopped sowing it. They held out in large numbers, fought off planters' gangs and refused to pay, led often by village headmen and better-off peasants.

The revolt came just after the Indian Rebellion of 1857, and the government, wary of more unrest, set up an Indigo Commission in 1860. It found widespread abuse and ruled that farmers could not be forced to grow the crop. Indigo in Bengal declined after that. The play Nil Darpan by Dinabandhu Mitra, showing the planters' cruelty, became famous. Indigo planting moved to Bihar, where Gandhi led a new campaign at Champaran in 1917.
sum: A rising of peasants in Bengal in 1859 and 1860 against European planters who forced them to grow indigo, the blue dye plant.
